dialogue.scene: Khalid tells his friend Sam about a winter camping trip in the desert that his family had planned for weeks.

p1.t: So, how was the camping trip? You'd been talking about it for weeks.
It could have gone better. A sandstorm arrived about an hour after we'd put up the tents.
Ah. So it wasn't exactly the relaxing weekend under the stars you'd promised everyone.
Not exactly, no. My uncle spent most of the night chasing a tent across the dunes.
That sounds a tad stressful, to put it mildly.

p2.t: And the 'luxury' camp my brother booked for the second night left a lot to be desired.
Why do I get the feeling 'luxury' is doing a lot of work in that sentence?
Let's just say the hot shower was more of a rumour than a reality.
Still, nobody got hurt, so it's not the end of the world.
True. And my grandfather says it was the best trip in years. I'm not sure he was joking.

dialogue.focus: So it wasn't exactly the relaxing weekend under the stars you'd promised everyone.
qs: What actually happened on the first night, and how does Khalid describe it?

culture.title: British Understatement
points: In 1912, the explorer Lawrence Oates walked out of his tent into an Antarctic blizzard, saying only, 'I am just going outside and may be some time.'
In British English, 'not bad' can mean 'very good', while 'quite good' can sound disappointing, depending on the tone.
Arabic speakers also soften bad news, often by stressing first that everyone is safe and well.
qs: Why do you think people choose to understate serious problems?
Can understatement cause misunderstandings? Give an example.

0-0.exit: Describe something that went wrong recently in two sentences, using understatement instead of complaining.

dialogue.scene: Noura is on a summer internship at an engineering company in Dammam. She tells her cousin Hessa about her manager's comments on her first report.

p1.t: My manager read my report and said, 'You might want to check the figures in section three.' That's all.
Reading between the lines, I'd say there's a mistake in section three.
I thought so too. Then he said, 'It's worth bearing in mind that the client reads everything very carefully.'
He's dropping a hint, Noura. He wants it checked thoroughly before it leaves the office.

p2.t: And at four o'clock he said, 'I wonder if we could have the final version by tomorrow morning.'
That's not really a question, is it?
Hardly. So I took the hint and stayed until six to finish it.
Good. Did he say anything about it this morning?
He said, 'This is much clearer.' From him, that's practically a standing ovation.

dialogue.focus: Reading between the lines, I'd say there's a mistake in section three.
qs: What did the manager really mean by 'You might want to check the figures'?

culture.title: Reading the Air
points: In Japanese, 'kuuki wo yomu', or 'reading the air', means sensing what others want without being told.
The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described 'high-context' cultures, where much of a message lies in the situation rather than the words.
Many Gulf workplaces also value indirect feedback, because it protects a colleague's dignity and keeps relationships smooth.
qs: Do you prefer direct or indirect feedback? Why?
What problems can indirect feedback cause in an international team?

dialogue.scene: Faisal and his classmate Emma are working on a group project. They discuss a message from Majed in the group chat.

p1.t: Did you see Majed's message? 'Great, another deadline moved forward. Best week ever.'
I did. I almost took it at face value and replied, 'Glad you're happy!'
Oh, that would have gone down well. He's clearly being sarcastic.
I know that now. The trouble is, Majed has such a dry sense of humour that it's hard to tell.

p2.t: In person, it's obvious. His deadpan face gives it away.
But in a text, the tone gets completely lost in translation.
Maybe we should suggest he adds an emoji when he's being tongue-in-cheek.
Or maybe we should ban sarcasm in the group chat altogether. I'm only half joking.
Oh yes, because banning things always works so well with teenagers.

dialogue.focus: Oh, that would have gone down well.
qs: Why did Faisal almost reply 'Glad you're happy!'?

That's good, isn't it? Punctuality matters.
It's faint praise, Yousef. Any mention of your actual chemistry is conspicuous by its absence.

p2.t: So the subtext is that I'm a nice person but an average student?
I'm not saying he thinks you're average, but a committee might read it that way.
It speaks volumes that he didn't mention my project, doesn't it?
It does. Use the physics letter, and maybe ask Mr Adel what he really thought.
Something tells me that conversation won't exactly be relaxing.

culture.title: Kinaya in Arabic Rhetoric
points: Classical Arabic rhetoric describes 'kinaya': expressing an idea indirectly through a related detail or image.
A traditional example praises a generous host as having 'plenty of ash', implying that his fire cooks for many guests.
English uses similar indirection: a reference that praises only someone's handwriting may imply that their work is weak.
qs: Why might indirect criticism sometimes be kinder than direct criticism?
Can you think of a Saudi expression that says something indirectly?

dialogue.scene: Omar and Tariq are writing a short comedy sketch for their school's drama evening. Every line must hide its real meaning.

p1.t: Scene one: a grandfather tastes his grandson's first attempt at kabsa. What does he say?
'Well, it's certainly… different.' He's far too kind to say it's awful.
Perfect. The audience will read between the lines straight away.
Then the grandson gets the wrong end of the stick and offers to cook every Friday.
And the grandfather replies, 'Let's not rush into anything.'

p2.t: Next, the mother walks in and says, 'How nice of you to tidy the kitchen afterwards.'
A loaded remark, because the kitchen is a disaster.

Her face will tell them. What she's really saying is 'Clean up now.'

culture.title: Irony on the Page and Stage

dialogue.scene: Reem is leading a student seminar on how Gulf cities can stay cool as summers get hotter. She opens the discussion with Ali and Hannah.

p1.t: Shall we kick off? To set the scene, today's article argues that our cities trap heat long after sunset.
Because of all the concrete and asphalt, presumably?
Partly. But I'd frame the question slightly differently: is the problem the materials, or the way we plan streets?
That's the crux of the matter, I think. Old neighbourhoods had narrow, shaded lanes for a reason.

p2.t: Good. I'd like to open the floor now. Ali, where do you stand?
For the sake of argument, let's say we can't rebuild whole cities. What can we change quickly?
Trees and shade structures, surely. They're relatively cheap.
So we already have two angles: long-term planning and quick fixes. Let's take them one at a time.
Sounds good. Could we start with the quick fixes? They're easier to picture.

culture.title: The Harkness Table
points: At Phillips Exeter Academy in the USA, classes have been taught around a single oval table since the 1930s, an approach called the Harkness method.
The teacher says as little as possible, while students lead the discussion and build on each other's ideas.
The Saudi majlis has a similar spirit: people sit together facing one another and exchange views in turn.

dialogue.scene: Majed is leading a seminar on whether local dialects are worth protecting. Tom has been talking for five minutes, and Leena hasn't spoken yet.

p1.t: …and that's why I think dialects will simply disappear. Honestly, that's how languages have always worked.
Thanks, Tom. You've clearly given this a lot of thought. I'd like to hear from a few other people too.
Sure, sorry. I do tend to hold the floor.
Not at all. Leena, you mentioned your grandmother's Nabati poems earlier. Would you like to come in on this?

p2.t: I would, if I can get a word in edgeways. Those poems only really work in the dialect.
That's a powerful example. Could you build on that? What exactly would be lost?
The rhythm, the humour, the local references. Standard Arabic can't carry all of it.
Tom, does that change your view at all? And anyone else is welcome to chip in.
It does, slightly. Maybe 'disappear' was too strong.

culture.title: Languages at Risk
points: Linguists estimate that thousands of the world's roughly 7,000 languages could disappear this century.
Nabati poetry, composed in the spoken Arabic of the Arabian Peninsula, has been passed down for centuries, often by word of mouth.
Arabic is one of the six official languages of the United Nations, and World Arabic Language Day is marked on 18 December.
qs: Is it worth protecting a dialect that fewer and fewer people speak? Why?
How could young people help keep local poetry alive?

dialogue.scene: Noor is leading a seminar on how Saudi Arabia can use water more sustainably. The discussion keeps drifting.

p1.t: Speaking of water, has anyone been to the new aquarium in Jeddah? The sharks are huge.
Sounds amazing, but I think we've gone off on a tangent. Let me bring us back to water use at home.
Right. The reading says a large share of our drinking water comes from desalination.
And the plants use a lot of energy. Actually, did you know the first plant on the Red Sea coast was…
Interesting, but let's park that point for now, or we'll get bogged down in history.

p2.t: Sorry, I've lost the thread a little. What's the main question again?
Whether changing household habits can make a real difference, or whether only technology can.
Then I'd say both. Shorter showers matter, but so do cleaner, cheaper plants.
Good. Ziad, I promise we'll come back to the history point at the end, if there's time.
Fair enough. I'll save my shark facts for the break.

What is the main question of the seminar?

culture.title: Water from the Sea
points: Saudi Arabia is one of the world's largest producers of desalinated water.
Desalination turns seawater into drinking water, but older methods use a great deal of energy.
Many newer plants use reverse osmosis, which pushes water through fine membranes and usually needs less energy.
qs: Should households pay more for water to encourage saving? Why or why not?
Which matters more: changing habits or improving technology?

1-2.exit: Imagine your discussion has drifted. Say two sentences to bring it back on track without being rude.

dialogue.scene: Sultan is leading a seminar on whether new buildings in Riyadh should copy traditional Najdi style. Halfway through, he summarises the views so far.

p1.t: Mud-brick looks beautiful, but nobody wants to live like it's two hundred years ago.
Traditional designs actually kept homes cool, though: thick walls, small windows, shaded courtyards.
Fine, but you can't build a forty-storey office tower out of mud.
Let me recap before we go further. Broadly speaking, we've heard two positions.

p2.t: Bader sees traditional style as beautiful but impractical. Jack sees practical lessons in it, especially for heat. Does that do justice to you both?
That's the gist of it, yes.
So in a nutshell, the disagreement seems to boil down to this: copying the look, or learning from the logic.
I'd accept that summary. I'm against copying the look, not against learning from it.
Then perhaps we're closer than it seemed. Shall we test that with a real example?

dialogue.focus: Broadly speaking, we've heard two positions.

culture.title: Learning from Mud-Brick
points: At-Turaif in Diriyah, the mud-brick district that was the first capital of the Saudi state, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
Traditional Najdi houses used thick earthen walls, small windows and inner courtyards to stay cool in summer.
Architects around the world now study traditional buildings to design more energy-efficient homes.
qs: Should new buildings in your city look traditional, modern or both?
What can modern designers learn from older buildings?

dialogue.scene: Lina is leading a seminar on fast fashion. After hearing two strong views, she tries to combine them into one position.

p1.t: Cheap clothes let families on a budget dress well. I don't think anyone should feel guilty about that.
But clothes worn only a few times create mountains of waste.
True, though second-hand shops aren't an option for everyone.
Let me try to draw the threads together. What seems to be emerging is that you both care about fairness.

p2.t: Fairness to families and fairness to the planet, you mean?
Exactly. And your points dovetail with each other more than they clash: affordable clothes that last longer would satisfy both.
So the common ground is quality at a fair price, not simply 'buy less'.
Yes. Can we reconcile that with Emily's concern about waste?
If clothes last longer, there's less waste. That's a middle way I can live with.

dialogue.focus: What seems to be emerging is that you both care about fairness.

culture.title: Fashion That Lasts
points: The fashion industry produces huge amounts of textile waste, and much of it ends up in landfill.
Repair and resale apps have grown quickly as young people look for cheaper, greener clothes.
Traditional Saudi garments such as the thobe and the bisht are often worn for years, and a fine bisht may be handed down.
qs: Would you buy fewer, better clothes if they cost more at first?
Who is most responsible for reducing waste: shoppers, brands or governments?

dialogue.scene: Rakan chairs a student seminar on whether Arabizi, Arabic written in Latin letters and numbers, is a threat to Arabic. It is almost time to finish.

p1.t: We've got five minutes left, so let's take stock. A recurring theme has been convenience versus identity.
Right. Arabizi is quick to type, but I worry my younger cousins can't spell properly in Arabic.
In fairness to Arabizi, people use it in informal chats, not in essays.
Good point. Before we wrap up, I'd like to open the floor to anyone who hasn't spoken yet.

p2.t: Just one thing: Arabic keyboards are easy now, so the original reason for Arabizi has almost gone.
Thanks, Yara. Let me draw the threads together. Nobody here thinks Arabizi will replace Arabic.
Agreed.
The real concern is young learners. So perhaps our position is: informal Arabizi is harmless, provided schools keep standards high.
That's a fair synthesis. I'd sign up to that.
Me too, though I'd love a follow-up seminar on emojis.

dialogue.focus: Let me draw the threads together.

culture.title: Arabic in the Digital Age
points: Arabizi, which uses numbers such as 3 and 7 for Arabic sounds, spread with early mobile phones that had no Arabic keyboard.
Today, Arabic is one of the most widely used languages on the internet.
Saudi Arabia has established the King Salman Global Academy for the Arabic Language to promote and develop Arabic.
qs: Do you ever write in Arabizi? When and why?
How can Arabic stay strong in a world of English-language technology?

dialogue.scene: At a public forum in a Jeddah community centre, student representative Turki presents a plan for cycle lanes along a busy road. A resident, Mr Saleh, challenges him.

p1.t: Next question from the floor, please.
Why do you want to make life harder for every driver in Jeddah just to please a few cyclists?
With respect, that's a loaded question. It assumes the lanes help only 'a few cyclists'.
Well, don't they?
I'd reject the premise. The lanes are for walkers, runners and families too, and they could reduce short car trips.

p2.t: So you're saying drivers don't matter.
I'm afraid you're putting words in my mouth. For the record, I drive myself.
Mr Saleh, is your concern really cars versus bikes?
It's that we can't have both on the same road.
That's a false choice. Many cities have redesigned roads so that cars, bikes and pedestrians all fit safely.

dialogue.focus: I'd reject the premise.
qs: Why does Turki call Mr Saleh's first question 'loaded'?
What does Turki mean by 'a false choice'?

prompts.hint: Point out the loaded assumption and reject the premise calmly.

prompts.hint: Say they're putting words in your mouth, then state your real position 'for the record'.

culture.title: Speakers' Corner
points: Since the nineteenth century, people have gathered at Speakers' Corner in London's Hyde Park to give speeches and face questions from passers-by.
Speakers there must think fast, because members of the crowd often interrupt with loaded or hostile questions.
Debating clubs and competitions have become increasingly popular in Saudi schools and universities in recent years.
qs: Would you dare to speak at Speakers' Corner? Why or why not?
What is the best way to answer a rude question in public?

expressions.def: to present an issue in a different way

dialogue.scene: On the school podcast, presenter Laura interviews student Nawaf, who supports replacing some end-of-term exams with projects.

p1.t: Critics say replacing exams with projects just makes school easier. Isn't that the truth?
I'd look at it another way. The real question isn't easier or harder; it's what we actually want to measure.
But surely exams are the fairest test of knowledge?
They test memory under pressure, which matters. But at its core, education should prepare us for real work.

p2.t: So you admit projects are easier to cheat on.
That's a fair concern, but I think it misses the point. Any system can be abused; the issue is design.
Then how would you design it?
I'd shift the focus from the final product to the process: drafts, presentations and questions in person.
You've rather reframed the whole debate.
That was the idea. If we only ask 'easier or harder?', we'll never get a useful answer.

dialogue.focus: The real question isn't easier or harder; it's what we actually want to measure.
qs: How does Nawaf reframe the debate about exams?
How would Nawaf make projects harder to cheat on?

speakout.scene: You are interviewed on your school podcast about a plan to stop selling sweets in the school canteen. The interviewer keeps framing it as 'freedom versus health'.

prompts.q: Isn't this simply taking away students' freedom?

prompts.q: But teenagers can decide for themselves, can't they?
prompts.hint: Accept part of the point, then shift the focus to something bigger.

prompts.q: So, in one sentence, what is this debate really about?

culture.title: The Power of Framing
points: The linguist George Lakoff became well known for arguing that the way an issue is framed shapes how people think about it.
The same change can be described as 'a reform' or 'a cut', and each word pushes listeners towards a different conclusion.
Skilled debaters often succeed not by answering the question as asked, but by showing that a better question exists.
qs: Can you think of an issue that sounds completely different depending on how it is described?
Is reframing a question honest, or is it a way of avoiding it?

dialogue.scene: Student council president Lama faces tough questions from Ruba, editor of the school newspaper, about spending most of the budget on one trip to Ithra in Dhahran.

p1.t: You spent sixty percent of the budget on one trip. Isn't that irresponsible?
That's a fair challenge, and I'm happy to answer it. The trip reached every student in Year 11.
Only Year 11. What about everyone else? Or are you going to dodge the question?
Not at all. I'll concede the point that other years got less this term.

p2.t: So you admit it was a mistake?
No. Conceding a point isn't the same as admitting a mistake. Next term, the budget goes to Years 9 and 10.
Some students say you only care about your own year.
I understand the frustration, but I'll stand my ground: the trip was planned with the whole council.
You're very calm. Doesn't this interview rattle you at all?
Keeping my composure is part of the job. Getting rattled wouldn't help anyone.

dialogue.focus: That's a fair challenge, and I'm happy to answer it.
qs: Which point does Lama concede, and which does she defend?

speakout.scene: You organised a school fundraising event that raised less money than expected. Your teacher plays a tough reporter.

culture.title: Under Pressure on Air
points: Long interviews on British radio and television are known for tough follow-up questions that keep returning to the same point.
Media trainers advise speakers to pause, breathe and answer the question actually asked, rather than react to its tone.
Audiences often judge a speaker's confidence as much by calm body language as by the words used.

What helps you stay calm when someone criticises you?

dialogue.scene: In a public school debate on banning energy drinks for under-18s, Saud faces an opponent, Daniel, who quotes doubtful statistics.

p1.t: Ninety percent of students who failed last term drank energy drinks. Case closed.
I'd question that figure. How many students who passed also drank them?
That's not the point.
It's exactly the point. Without that comparison, you're mistaking correlation for causation.
Teenagers who drink them are simply less focused. Everyone knows that.

p2.t: That's a sweeping generalisation. Some athletes use them carefully before training.
But a doctor on the news said they were dangerous.
She said they were dangerous in large amounts. You've taken her words out of context.
So you think they're harmless?
No. The evidence points to real risks for teenagers, but your statistics don't bear out your claim. Don't cherry-pick.

speakout.scene: Your teacher plays an opponent in a public debate on whether video games make teenagers aggressive, and quotes doubtful evidence.

culture.title: How to Lie with Statistics
points: In 1954, Darrell Huff published 'How to Lie with Statistics', a short book showing how numbers and graphs can mislead.

Fact-checking organisations around the world now test public claims against the original data.

dialogue.scene: Hamza and his friend Liam are preparing the closing speech for a public debate on whether their neighbourhood should turn a gravel lot into a shaded garden. Many residents are undecided.

p1.t: Half the audience hasn't decided yet. How do we win them over?

Like what? Lower temperatures? Fewer cars?
Children playing outside in the evening. Everyone remembers doing that.

p2.t: And the residents who are worried about parking?
We meet them halfway: keep twenty spaces at the edge and plant trees in the rest.
Then we should end with the bigger picture, not just our street.
Exactly: 'We're not asking you to choose between cars and children. We're asking you to make common cause with your neighbours.'
That makes a compelling case. Even the parking group might clap.

dialogue.scene: At a public debate in a cultural centre, Ahmed argues that popular heritage sites should limit daily visitor numbers. His opponent, Kate, and a sceptical audience member, Mr Hassan, challenge him.

p1.t: Limiting visitors is elitist. Only the rich will ever get tickets.
I'd reject the premise that limits mean high prices. Many sites use free timed slots booked online.
Isn't this just playing to the gallery? Everyone loves 'protecting heritage'.
That's a fair challenge. But the real question is whether these sites survive for our grandchildren.

p2.t: Fewer visitors means less money for local businesses.
Let me turn the tables: what happens to local businesses if the site is damaged and has to close?
That's a worst-case scenario.
It's a real one. Venice has started charging day-trippers on its busiest days for exactly that reason.
Well, you've held your own, I'll give you that. Let's hear your closing statement.

dialogue.focus: But the real question is whether these sites survive for our grandchildren.
qs: How does Ahmed answer the claim that limits are elitist?
How does Ahmed 'turn the tables' on Kate?

dialogue.scene: Ghada is practising for IELTS Speaking Part 3 with her tutor, Ms Clarke. The topic is public transport.

p1.t: How has public transport changed in your city?
By and large, it's improved enormously. The new metro is a far cry from the days when the car was the only option.
Good. Is congestion still a problem?
Yes, though to a lesser extent on the main routes. Rush hour still exacerbates things near schools.

p2.t: Nice. You said 'enormously'. Is that precise?
Perhaps not. 'Considerably' is more accurate; the effect on traffic so far has been modest, though certainly not negligible.
That's the kind of precision examiners reward. What about buses?
Bus connections are still a bit hit and miss: some areas are well served, others hardly at all.
Excellent. Your range is wide, but it's the accuracy that makes it Band 9.

dialogue.focus: The new metro is a far cry from the days when the car was the only option.

points: IELTS Speaking is assessed on four criteria: fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation.
At Band 9, candidates use vocabulary with full flexibility and precision, including idiomatic language used naturally.
The Riyadh Metro, which opened in stages from late 2024, is one of the largest urban rail projects in the region.

dialogue.scene: Mishal practises an IELTS Part 2 talk about a person who has influenced him. His friend Adam times him and gives feedback.

p1.t: Your topic: describe a person who has influenced you. You've got two minutes.
I'd like to talk about my football coach, Ibrahim, who has left a lasting impression on me.
How did you meet him?
I joined his academy at twelve. It was a steep learning curve; I'd never trained so seriously.
And what makes him special?
He always went the extra mile, staying late to help weaker players. That attitude has rubbed off on me.

p2.t: Time's up. That sounded natural. But did you use too many idioms?
I don't think so. Each one fitted. I avoided anything like 'raining cats and dogs'.
Good call. You wanted to use 'come into my own' as well.
I'll add it: I really came into my own as captain once Coach Ibrahim trusted me.
And you've taken my criticism in your stride. That's another idiom, by the way.

dialogue.focus: That attitude has rubbed off on me.
qs: Why does Mishal say joining the academy was 'a steep learning curve'?

culture.title: Natural Idiom, Not Decoration
points: IELTS examiners reward idiomatic language only when it is accurate and suits the context.
Many learners memorise idioms like 'raining cats and dogs', which most native speakers rarely use today.
In Arabic, too, one well-chosen proverb impresses, while a string of them sounds rehearsed.
qs: Which English idiom do you find most useful? Why?
Is there an Arabic proverb you'd like to translate into English? Which one?

3-1.exit: Tell me about someone who influenced you in two sentences, using two idioms naturally.

dialogue.scene: Razan is preparing for the C2 Proficiency speaking test. Her teacher, Mr Davies, gives her a long-turn question: 'Is technology making our memories weaker?'

p1.t: Here's your question: 'Is technology making our memories weaker?' About two minutes, please.
It stands to reason that if our phones store everything, we practise remembering less. Phone numbers are a case in point.
Good start. Keep going.
But technology also frees our memory for deeper thinking, not least because we can find facts instantly.
Good. Anything else?

p2.t: By the same token, apps can train memory: language apps use repetition far better than notebooks did.
And your conclusion?
On balance, technology is a double-edged sword: it weakens some kinds of memory but strengthens our ability to find and use information.
Very well structured. At C2, examiners want a clear position, not just a list.
Then I'll state it more firmly: I'd say the benefits slightly outweigh the costs.

dialogue.focus: On balance, technology is a double-edged sword: it weakens some kinds of memory but strengthens our ability to find and use information.
qs: What example does Razan give to support her first point?
What advice does Mr Davies give about her conclusion?

culture.title: The 'Google Effect'
points: In 2011, a study led by psychologist Betsy Sparrow suggested that people remember less when they expect to find information online later.
Researchers sometimes call this the 'Google effect' or 'digital amnesia'.
Long before the internet, scholars in the Arab world trained remarkable memories, and many could recite long poems by heart.
qs: Should schools still ask students to memorise poems or facts? Why?
Is it a problem if we remember where to find information rather than the information itself?

3-2.exit: In two sentences, give a balanced view on whether technology helps or harms learning, ending with 'On balance, …'.

dialogue.scene: Bassam and his friend Nick are practising abstract IELTS Part 3 questions about success and happiness.

p1.t: Here's one: 'Is success the same thing as happiness?'
In the broadest sense, no. Success is usually measured against other people; happiness isn't.
But they're connected, surely?
For some people they're inextricably linked, but it's debatable whether one causes the other.

p2.t: So what does happiness hinge on, in your view?
Largely on relationships, I'd say. A long-running Harvard study of adult life found much the same.
And money?
It's a matter of degree. Enough money removes stress; beyond that, it seems to add surprisingly little.
That's a Band 9 answer, I think: abstract, but grounded in evidence.

dialogue.focus: It's a matter of degree.
qs: How does Bassam distinguish success from happiness?
What, according to Bassam, does happiness mainly hinge on?

culture.title: What Makes a Good Life?
points: The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed participants since 1938 and found that close relationships strongly predict long-term wellbeing.
Saudi Vision 2030 includes a Quality of Life Program that supports sport, culture and entertainment.
Arabic has a word, 'qana'a', for the contentment of being satisfied with what you have.

Can a country make its people happier? How?

dialogue.scene: During a mock C2 speaking test, Abeer describes Al Sadu weaving to the examiner, Mrs Ward, and repairs her language when she gets stuck.

p1.t: Tell me about a traditional craft from your country.
I'd like to talk about Al Sadu, a type of weaving done by Bedouin women, or rather, traditionally done by them.
What do they make?
Tents, cushions and the… the word escapes me… the long woven pieces that divide a tent inside.
Dividers?

p2.t: Yes, dividers. The patterns are, for want of a better word, a kind of language.
In what sense?
Let me rephrase that. What I'm getting at is that the patterns carry meaning about the weaver's family and surroundings.
Interesting. Is it still practised today?
Yes, though less widely. To be more precise, UNESCO listed it in 2020 as heritage in urgent need of safeguarding.

dialogue.focus: What I'm getting at is that the patterns carry meaning about the weaver's family and surroundings.
qs: How does Abeer manage when she can't find a word?
Why does Abeer compare the patterns to a language?

culture.title: Al Sadu Weaving
points: Al Sadu is a traditional form of weaving practised by Bedouin women in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
Weavers use wool from sheep, camels and goats, often in bold geometric patterns of red, black and white.
In 2020, UNESCO added Al Sadu to its list of intangible heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.
qs: Why do traditional crafts disappear, and should we try to save them?
Would you like to learn a traditional craft? Which one?

3-4.exit: Describe an object whose English name you don't know, using two repair phrases from today.

dialogue.scene: Talal sits a full mock IELTS Speaking test with his teacher, Ms Patel. They have reached Part 3, on cities of the future.

p1.t: Part 3 now. What will cities look like in fifty years?
That's a tricky one. Off the top of my head, I'd say greener, quieter and far more walkable.
Why walkable?
Because health and urban design go hand in hand. Car-centred cities are a far cry from what planners want now.

p2.t: Some people say technology will solve every urban problem. Do you agree?
By and large, no. Technology helps, but cities also need to strike a balance between innovation and community life.
Could you give an example?
The '15-minute city' is a case in point: shops, schools and parks within a short walk, whatever the technology.
And your overall view?
On balance, the best future cities will be designed around people rather than machines.

dialogue.focus: On balance, the best future cities will be designed around people rather than machines.
qs: Why does Talal think future cities will be more walkable?
What example does Talal give, and what point does it support?

prompts.q: Part 2: Describe a place in your city that has changed a lot.
prompts.hint: Speak for up to two minutes, using precise vocabulary and one or two natural idioms.

prompts.q: Part 3: Should cities be designed for cars or for people?
prompts.hint: Give a balanced answer, repair yourself smoothly if needed, and finish with 'On balance, …'.

culture.title: The 15-Minute City
points: The '15-minute city', an idea popularised by urbanist Carlos Moreno, puts daily needs within a short walk or bike ride.
Paris is one of several cities that have adopted ideas from the 15-minute city model.
Saudi cities are adding parks, walking trails and public transport to make neighbourhoods more liveable.
qs: Is your neighbourhood a '15-minute neighbourhood'? What is missing?
Would you give up a car to live in a walkable city? Why?

3-5.exit: Answer this Part 3 question in three sentences at Band 9: 'How will technology change the way we live in cities?'

dialogue.t: So, how was the camping trip? You'd been talking about it for weeks.
It could have gone better. A sandstorm arrived about an hour after we'd put up the tents.
Ah. So it wasn't exactly the relaxing weekend under the stars you'd promised everyone.
Not exactly, no. My uncle spent most of the night chasing a tent across the dunes.
And the 'luxury' camp my brother booked for the second night left a lot to be desired.
Let's just say the hot shower was more of a rumour than a reality.
Still, nobody got hurt, so it's not the end of the world.

words.ex: Reading between the lines, the manager wasn't happy with the report.
She dropped a hint that she wanted a new laptop.
He didn't take the hint and stayed for another two hours.
You might want to check the figures again.
I wonder if we could start a little earlier tomorrow.
It's worth bearing in mind that the client is very particular.

dialogue.t: My manager read my report and said, 'You might want to check the figures in section three.' That's all.
Reading between the lines, I'd say there's a mistake in section three.
I thought so too. Then he said, 'It's worth bearing in mind that the client reads everything very carefully.'
He's dropping a hint, Noura. He wants it checked thoroughly before it leaves the office.
And at four o'clock he said, 'I wonder if we could have the final version by tomorrow morning.'
Hardly. So I took the hint and stayed until six to finish it.
He said, 'This is much clearer.' From him, that's practically a standing ovation.

grammar.title: Tentative hints
grammar.ar: للنصح أو الطلب بلطف نستخدم صيغاً غير مباشرة، لكن المعنى الحقيقي أقوى من الكلمات: you might want to تعني غالباً «يجب أن».
examples: You might want to proofread this again.
I wonder if you could send it by noon.
It's worth bearing in mind that he's always punctual.

words.ex: Her review was tongue-in-cheek, but some readers took it seriously.
He delivered the joke in a perfectly deadpan voice.
Don't take everything she says at face value.
Much of the irony got lost in translation.
I'm only half joking when I say I'll never cook again.
Our physics teacher has a very dry sense of humour.

dialogue.t: Did you see Majed's message? 'Great, another deadline moved forward. Best week ever.'
I did. I almost took it at face value and replied, 'Glad you're happy!'
Oh, that would have gone down well. He's clearly being sarcastic.
I know that now. The trouble is, Majed has such a dry sense of humour that it's hard to tell.
In person, it's obvious. His deadpan face gives it away.
But in a text, the tone gets completely lost in translation.
Or maybe we should ban sarcasm in the group chat altogether. I'm only half joking.

Well, that went well. (after a disaster)

I'm not saying he copied it, but the two essays are remarkably similar.

He says you're 'always punctual and very polite'. That's it.
It's faint praise, Yousef. Any mention of your actual chemistry is conspicuous by its absence.
So the subtext is that I'm a nice person but an average student?
I'm not saying he thinks you're average, but a committee might read it that way.
It speaks volumes that he didn't mention my project, doesn't it?
It does. Use the physics letter, and maybe ask Mr Adel what he really thought.

Probably. But he did leave the door open for the match.

dialogue.t: Scene one: a grandfather tastes his grandson's first attempt at kabsa. What does he say?
'Well, it's certainly… different.' He's far too kind to say it's awful.
Then the grandson gets the wrong end of the stick and offers to cook every Friday.
And the grandfather replies, 'Let's not rush into anything.'
Next, the mother walks in and says, 'How nice of you to tidy the kitchen afterwards.'
A loaded remark, because the kitchen is a disaster.
Her face will tell them. What she's really saying is 'Clean up now.'

grammar.title: Layering meaning
grammar.ar: نجمع أدوات الوحدة: التهوين والتهكم والتلميح، ثم نشرح المعنى المقصود بعبارة What he's really saying is …
examples: 'It's certainly… different.' (= I don't like it.)
'Nice of you to join us.' (= You're late.)
What she's really saying is that we should leave.

words.ex: Shall we kick off with the main reading?
To set the scene, let me summarise the article.
How we frame the question shapes the whole discussion.
Cost is the crux of the matter.
After my introduction, I'll open the floor.
For the sake of argument, imagine the budget is unlimited.

dialogue.t: Shall we kick off? To set the scene, today's article argues that our cities trap heat long after sunset.
Partly. But I'd frame the question slightly differently: is the problem the materials, or the way we plan streets?
That's the crux of the matter, I think. Old neighbourhoods had narrow, shaded lanes for a reason.
Good. I'd like to open the floor now. Ali, where do you stand?
For the sake of argument, let's say we can't rebuild whole cities. What can we change quickly?
So we already have two angles: long-term planning and quick fixes. Let's take them one at a time.
Sounds good. Could we start with the quick fixes? They're easier to picture.

grammar.title: Opening a discussion
grammar.ar: لافتتاح النقاش: نبدأ، نعرض الخلفية، نصوغ السؤال الأساسي بدقة، ثم نفتح باب المشاركة.

I would, if I can get a word in edgeways. Those poems only really work in the dialect.
That's a powerful example. Could you build on that? What exactly would be lost?
Tom, does that change your view at all? And anyone else is welcome to chip in.
It does, slightly. Maybe 'disappear' was too strong.

grammar.title: Inviting and managing turns
grammar.ar: لإشراك الجميع بلطف: نشكر من يطيل الكلام، ثم ندعو غيره بالاسم ونطلب منه التوسّع.

Good. Ziad, I promise we'll come back to the history point at the end, if there's time.
Fair enough. I'll save my shark facts for the break.

grammar.title: Steering a discussion
grammar.ar: لإعادة النقاش إلى مساره بلطف: نعترف بالفكرة، ثم نؤجّلها، ثم نعيد طرح السؤال الرئيس.

So in a nutshell, the disagreement seems to boil down to this: copying the look, or learning from the logic.
I'd accept that summary. I'm against copying the look, not against learning from it.

grammar.title: Summarising views
grammar.ar: للتلخيص بإنصاف: نعرض المواقف باختصار، ثم نحدد جوهر الخلاف، ونتأكد أن أصحابها يوافقون على تلخيصنا.

dialogue.t: Cheap clothes let families on a budget dress well. I don't think anyone should feel guilty about that.
But clothes worn only a few times create mountains of waste.
Let me try to draw the threads together. What seems to be emerging is that you both care about fairness.
Exactly. And your points dovetail with each other more than they clash: affordable clothes that last longer would satisfy both.
So the common ground is quality at a fair price, not simply 'buy less'.
Yes. Can we reconcile that with Emily's concern about waste?
If clothes last longer, there's less waste. That's a middle way I can live with.

grammar.ar: التركيب أعلى من التلخيص: لا نعدّد الآراء فقط، بل نجمعها في موقف واحد يُبرز الأرضية المشتركة ويوفّق بينها.

Good point. Before we wrap up, I'd like to open the floor to anyone who hasn't spoken yet.
Thanks, Yara. Let me draw the threads together. Nobody here thinks Arabizi will replace Arabic.
The real concern is young learners. So perhaps our position is: informal Arabizi is harmless, provided schools keep standards high.
That's a fair synthesis. I'd sign up to that.

dialogue.t: Why do you want to make life harder for every driver in Jeddah just to please a few cyclists?
With respect, that's a loaded question. It assumes the lanes help only 'a few cyclists'.
Well, don't they?
I'd reject the premise. The lanes are for walkers, runners and families too, and they could reduce short car trips.
So you're saying drivers don't matter.
I'm afraid you're putting words in my mouth. For the record, I drive myself.
That's a false choice. Many cities have redesigned roads so that cars, bikes and pedestrians all fit safely.

grammar.title: Rejecting a premise
grammar.ar: السؤال المُحمَّل يفترض أمراً غير صحيح؛ نكشف الافتراض ونرفضه بهدوء قبل أن نجيب.

dialogue.t: Critics say replacing exams with projects just makes school easier. Isn't that the truth?
I'd look at it another way. The real question isn't easier or harder; it's what we actually want to measure.
They test memory under pressure, which matters. But at its core, education should prepare us for real work.
So you admit projects are easier to cheat on.
That's a fair concern, but I think it misses the point. Any system can be abused; the issue is design.
I'd shift the focus from the final product to the process: drafts, presentations and questions in person.
That was the idea. If we only ask 'easier or harder?', we'll never get a useful answer.

grammar.title: Reframing
grammar.ar: إعادة التأطير: لا نقبل إطار السؤال كما طُرح، بل ننقل النقاش إلى السؤال الأهم.

dialogue.t: You spent sixty percent of the budget on one trip. Isn't that irresponsible?
That's a fair challenge, and I'm happy to answer it. The trip reached every student in Year 11.
Only Year 11. What about everyone else? Or are you going to dodge the question?
Not at all. I'll concede the point that other years got less this term.
No. Conceding a point isn't the same as admitting a mistake. Next term, the budget goes to Years 9 and 10.
I understand the frustration, but I'll stand my ground: the trip was planned with the whole council.
Keeping my composure is part of the job. Getting rattled wouldn't help anyone.

grammar.title: Conceding and holding firm

I'd question that figure. How many students who passed also drank them?
It's exactly the point. Without that comparison, you're mistaking correlation for causation.
That's a sweeping generalisation. Some athletes use them carefully before training.
But a doctor on the news said they were dangerous.
She said they were dangerous in large amounts. You've taken her words out of context.
No. The evidence points to real risks for teenagers, but your statistics don't bear out your claim. Don't cherry-pick.

Facts alone won't do it. We need something that strikes a chord with families.
Children playing outside in the evening. Everyone remembers doing that.
And the residents who are worried about parking?
We meet them halfway: keep twenty spaces at the edge and plant trees in the rest.
Exactly: 'We're not asking you to choose between cars and children. We're asking you to make common cause with your neighbours.'
That makes a compelling case. Even the parking group might clap.

grammar.title: Persuading the undecided
grammar.ar: لكسب الجمهور المتردد: نلامس قيمه، ونقدّم حلاً وسطاً لمخاوفه، ثم نختم بالصورة الأشمل.

I'd reject the premise that limits mean high prices. Many sites use free timed slots booked online.
Isn't this just playing to the gallery? Everyone loves 'protecting heritage'.
That's a fair challenge. But the real question is whether these sites survive for our grandchildren.
Let me turn the tables: what happens to local businesses if the site is damaged and has to close?
It's a real one. Venice has started charging day-trippers on its busiest days for exactly that reason.
Well, you've held your own, I'll give you that. Let's hear your closing statement.

grammar.title: Debating under pressure
grammar.ar: في المناظرة العامة: نرفض الافتراضات الخاطئة، ونعيد التأطير، ونقلب الحجة على الخصم، ثم نختم بكلمة قوية.

dialogue.t: How has public transport changed in your city?
By and large, it's improved enormously. The new metro is a far cry from the days when the car was the only option.
Yes, though to a lesser extent on the main routes. Rush hour still exacerbates things near schools.
Nice. You said 'enormously'. Is that precise?
Perhaps not. 'Considerably' is more accurate; the effect on traffic so far has been modest, though certainly not negligible.
Bus connections are still a bit hit and miss: some areas are well served, others hardly at all.
Excellent. Your range is wide, but it's the accuracy that makes it Band 9.

grammar.title: Precision in word choice

dialogue.t: I'd like to talk about my football coach, Ibrahim, who has left a lasting impression on me.
I joined his academy at twelve. It was a steep learning curve; I'd never trained so seriously.
He always went the extra mile, staying late to help weaker players. That attitude has rubbed off on me.
Time's up. That sounded natural. But did you use too many idioms?
I don't think so. Each one fitted. I avoided anything like 'raining cats and dogs'.
Good call. You wanted to use 'come into my own' as well.
I'll add it: I really came into my own as captain once Coach Ibrahim trusted me.

dialogue.t: Here's your question: 'Is technology making our memories weaker?' About two minutes, please.
It stands to reason that if our phones store everything, we practise remembering less. Phone numbers are a case in point.
But technology also frees our memory for deeper thinking, not least because we can find facts instantly.
By the same token, apps can train memory: language apps use repetition far better than notebooks did.
And your conclusion?
On balance, technology is a double-edged sword: it weakens some kinds of memory but strengthens our ability to find and use information.
Very well structured. At C2, examiners want a clear position, not just a list.

dialogue.t: Here's one: 'Is success the same thing as happiness?'
In the broadest sense, no. Success is usually measured against other people; happiness isn't.
For some people they're inextricably linked, but it's debatable whether one causes the other.
So what does happiness hinge on, in your view?
Largely on relationships, I'd say. A long-running Harvard study of adult life found much the same.
And money?
It's a matter of degree. Enough money removes stress; beyond that, it seems to add surprisingly little.

In what sense?
